case_info.scenario: A 19-year-old man was referred for evaluation of bilateral retinal detachments. His visual acuity with correction on a Snellen chart was 20/400 and 20/500 in the right and left eyes, respectively. Anterior examination revealed no anterior chamber cells and well-dilated iris with clear lens in both eyes. Posterior examination showed no vitreous cells, hyperemic and elevated discs, macular edema, and large inferior serous detachments with deep, creamy lesions throughout the posterior pole in both eyes (Figure). No retinal breaks were observed in either eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated subretinal and intraretinal fluid in the macula of both eyes, with a subfoveal bacillary detachment, ie, a splitting at the level of the inner segments of the photoreceptors. B-scan ultrasound confirmed retinal detachments in both eyes with no choroidal masses or detachment. Medical history included attention-deficit/hyperactive disorder, for which he took dextroamphetamine (Adderall) since childhood. The patient noted that vision was progressively worsening starting 1 week prior to presentation, during which time he was recovering from an upper respiratory tract illness and diarrhea that self-resolved. Review of systems was otherwise negative for any headache, altered mental status, chest pain, tinnitus, urinary issues, or trauma prior to presentation.

case_info.explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.

case_info.caption: Red-free fundus photographs demonstrating large serous detachments and deep subretinal lesions (arrowheads) with optical coherence tomography B-scan confirming the detachment. A, Right eye. B, Left eye.
case_info.explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.

Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. case_info.explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.caption: Red-free fundus photographs demonstrating large serous detachments and deep subretinal lesions (arrowheads) with optical coherence tomography B-scan confirming the detachment. A, Right eye. B, Left eye.
case_info.explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.

case_info.explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

case_info.scenario: A 19-year-old man was referred for evaluation of bilateral retinal detachments. His visual acuity with correction on a Snellen chart was 20/400 and 20/500 in the right and left eyes, respectively. Anterior examination revealed no anterior chamber cells and well-dilated iris with clear lens in both eyes. Posterior examination showed no vitreous cells, hyperemic and elevated discs, macular edema, and large inferior serous detachments with deep, creamy lesions throughout the posterior pole in both eyes (Figure). No retinal breaks were observed in either eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated subretinal and intraretinal fluid in the macula of both eyes, with a subfoveal bacillary detachment, ie, a splitting at the level of the inner segments of the photoreceptors. B-scan ultrasound confirmed retinal detachments in both eyes with no choroidal masses or detachment. Medical history included attention-deficit/hyperactive disorder, for which he took dextroamphetamine (Adderall) since childhood. The patient noted that vision was progressively worsening starting 1 week prior to presentation, during which time he was recovering from an upper respiratory tract illness and diarrhea that self-resolved. Review of systems was otherwise negative for any headache, altered mental status, chest pain, tinnitus, urinary issues, or trauma prior to presentation.

case_info.explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.
